title: Accessible Amateur Radio: Practical Ways to Get On Air | ZL3TOM
description: Practical amateur radio options for disabled operators: accessible controls, screen readers, communication choices, comfortable station layouts and support from clubs.
keywords: accessible amateur radio, disabled radio operators, screen readers, adaptive PTT, inclusive ham radio, ZL3TOM
content: ZL3TOM beginner guide Accessible Amateur Radio: Practical Ways to Get On Air Practical amateur radio options for disabled operators: accessible controls, screen readers, communication choices, comfortable station layouts and support from clubs. ← All guides 01 Radio should make room for different people Disability does not describe a single set of needs. Mobility, dexterity, sight, hearing, speech, fatigue, sensory needs and learning preferences can all affect how someone operates. Start with what you want to do and the adjustments that work for you. You do not need an expensive station to begin exploring. Listening, learning, digital contacts and internet-linked systems offer different routes into the hobby. Ask about licensing and operating requirements for the activity you choose. 02 Make your station comfortable to operate Keep essential controls within a comfortable reach. A stable desk, supported microphone and clearly organised cables can reduce handling. Try a larger PTT button or supported keyboard control if gripping a handheld is difficult. Check how transmit stops and choose a setup you can release reliably. Use a headset, desk microphone or speaker arrangement that suits your hearing, posture and comfort. Ask for help with mounting equipment or antenna work that is difficult to do safely. Plan breaks and shorter sessions if concentration or fatigue makes long nets difficult. A switch, microphone or adapter must be compatible with the equipment or app. Try before buying where possible. 03 Screen readers, low vision and software radio Look for software with labelled controls, keyboard navigation, readable status messages and adjustable text. Try your own screen reader with the actual app before relying on it; features and accessibility can differ between versions. Windows users may use Narrator or NVDA, Android users TalkBack, and Apple users VoiceOver. Browser zoom, magnification and operating-system contrast settings may also help. QSO One can access several amateur voice networks using a computer or Android device without a separate radio or hotspot. That may reduce physical handling, but it is not a promise that every QSO One control works with every assistive technology. Test sign-in, destination selection, PTT and disconnect first. 04 Choose a communication method that suits you Voice is one option. If speech or hearing makes voice contacts difficult, explore text-based amateur modes and ask a club about compatible software and equipment. Different systems have different requirements, and a chat feature in a voice app is not necessarily carried to radio listeners. For voice, prepare a short callsign and introduction, ask people to slow down or repeat details, and tell net control what accommodation would help. You decide how much personal information to share. OPTIONAL REQUEST This is ZL3TOM. Please allow me a little extra time to reply. Thank you. For hearing access, try clear audio at a comfortable level and compatible equipment. Captions or transcriptions may help where available, but check important callsigns and messages because automatic text can be wrong. 05 Ask clubs and net organisers for practical adjustments Ask about step-free access, accessible toilets, parking close to the venue, seating, quiet space, written instructions and remote participation before visiting. A support person can help with setup or access; the station operator remains responsible for the required operating authorisation. Smaller conversations, written setup steps and a named person to contact can make a first session less overwhelming. A good starting point is the clubs and community page . Explain the adjustment you need rather than feeling obliged to disclose a diagnosis. 06 Using this website This site includes a skip-to-content link, keyboard controls, visible focus, labelled fields, text alternatives and reduced-motion styles. On the Guides page , browse topic sections or use the category and title filters. Calculator results are announced through status messages without moving your focus. Use your browser’s zoom or device accessibility settings to adjust reading size. Press Tab to move between controls, Enter to follow links, and Escape to close the navigation or search dialog. Embedded videos and third-party services have their own accessibility behaviour. If something blocks you, send website feedback to Thomas . Include the page, what you were trying to do, and your browser or assistive technology if you are comfortable sharing it. This site has not been independently certified for accessibility; practical feedback helps guide further improvements. Official sources Software and network details change. content: ZL3TOM beginner guide AllStarLink for Beginners: Nodes and Good Operating Understand AllStarLink nodes, linked radio contacts, connecting and disconnecting, operator etiquette, basic node setup and security. ← All guides 01 What AllStarLink is AllStarLink connects amateur repeaters, remote-base stations and personal nodes using voice over IP. The network is based on Asterisk and the amateur-radio app_rpt system. A node normally has a unique number that operators use as its network address. 02 Nodes, links and the RF side Node A registered AllStar system identified by a node number. Link A network connection between two or more nodes. Radio interface Hardware that connects the node computer to a radio or repeater. Permanent connection A link configured to reconnect or remain connected; use only where the node owners permit it. 03 Make a linked contact Listen on the local node or repeater and identify any existing conversation. Use the connection method and control codes published by that node's owner. After connecting, pause so the network path can settle. Give your callsign, say which node you are using, and make a short call. Leave gaps between overs so another station can break in. Disconnect using the local node's documented command when you finish. DTMF commands vary. Never assume one node uses the same controls as another. 04 ZL3TOM node 40452 AllStar node 40452 and EchoLink node 304602 (ZL3TOM-L) are the two linked-radio nodes in my multimode system. Open the ZL3TOM AllStar Dashboard for node 40452 ↗ 05 If you want to build your own node Start with the current AllStarLink registration and installation information. A typical node needs a supported computer, a radio interface, suitable RF equipment, reliable power and internet, and correct audio and signalling configuration. Test locally at low power, confirm your audio levels and station identification, and follow the frequency coordination or band plan that applies in your area. 06 Keep the node secure Never publish IAX, SSH, web-admin or hotspot passwords. Keep the operating system and AllStar software updated. Restrict administration to trusted addresses or a VPN where practical. Back up the working configuration before making changes. Use only credentials and node numbers assigned or authorised for you. Official sources Software and network details change. content: ZL3TOM beginner guide Useful Amateur Radio Apps for Phone and Computer A practical guide to useful amateur radio apps for logging, programming, APRS, weak-signal modes, EchoLink and linked digital voice on phones and computers. ← All guides 01 Choose an app for a job The best radio app is the one that solves a clear problem. Start with one logger and the official programming software for your radio, then add tools as your operating interests grow. Platform support changes, so check each official download page before installing. Never enter radio-network credentials into an unknown app or website. 02 Programming: CHIRP CHIRP ↗ is a free, open-source tool that can program many amateur radios. It is useful for organising repeaters, simplex channels and memory names. Confirm that your exact radio model is supported. Use the correct data cable and driver. Download from the radio before editing. Save an untouched backup before uploading changes. 03 Weak-signal digital modes: WSJT-X WSJT-X ↗ is desktop software for weak-signal amateur radio communication. It is widely used for modes including FT8 and FT4. Accurate computer time, correct radio control, and clean audio levels matter. Check your licence conditions, band plan and frequency before transmitting. 04 APRS: APRSdroid and APRS.fi APRSdroid ↗ provides APRS features on Android, including position, nearby stations and messages. APRS.fi ↗ is a convenient browser map for looking up stations such as ZL3TOM ↗ . Think carefully before beaconing a home or private location. Only transmit on amateur frequencies if you are licensed and your setup follows local rules. 05 Portable logging: Ham2K PoLo Ham2K Portable Logger ↗ is designed for portable logging on Android and iOS. It can help organise activations and export contacts for your main log. After an activation, review callsigns, UTC times, bands and modes before uploading contacts to an online logbook. 06 Linked voice: EchoLink and QSO One EchoLink ↗ connects licensed operators and internet-linked stations. title: Amateur Radio Callsigns Explained: Prefixes, Suffixes and New Zealand Callsigns | ZL3TOM
description: Learn how amateur radio callsigns work, including prefixes, numbers, suffixes, New Zealand ZL callsigns, portable and mobile identifiers, and how to read international callsigns.

content: ZL3TOM amateur radio guide Amateur Radio Callsigns Explained: Prefixes, Suffixes and New Zealand Callsigns Learn how amateur radio callsigns work, including prefixes, numbers, suffixes, New Zealand ZL callsigns, portable and mobile identifiers, and how to read international callsigns. ← All guides What is an amateur radio callsign? A callsign is the on-air identifier assigned to an amateur-radio station or operator under the relevant licensing system. Callsigns let other operators identify who they are communicating with and often provide a clue about the country or territory associated with the station. Breaking a callsign into parts A callsign usually contains a prefix , a numeral and a suffix . In ZL3TOM , “ZL” identifies the New Zealand callsign series, “3” is the numeral, and “TOM” is the suffix. The exact meaning and allocation rules vary between administrations, so do not assume the numeral always identifies a present-day physical district. New Zealand callsigns New Zealand amateur callsigns commonly use the ZL prefix, with other prefixes or special-event callsigns also possible under New Zealand arrangements. For current licensing and callsign rules, use New Zealand's official radio-spectrum information and recognised amateur-radio organisations rather than relying on an old callsign list. International callsigns Prefixes are allocated internationally in blocks. Familiar examples include ZL for New Zealand stations, VK for Australia and many W, K, N and AA–AL series calls in the United States. A prefix is useful for recognising a likely country or territory, but special-event, reciprocal and portable operation can make the real operating location different. Portable and mobile identifiers You may hear operators describe themselves as portable , mobile or operating from another location. Written forms such as /P and /M are commonly seen, but the identification requirements that legally apply depend on the licensing jurisdiction and circumstances. Follow the rules that apply to your station rather than assuming one worldwide format. How to say a callsign clearly Use the ITU phonetic alphabet when conditions are difficult. ZL3TOM can be spoken as Zulu Lima Three Tango Oscar Mike . Say it at a natural pace and repeat it when needed. Why did I hear a different prefix? An operator may be visiting another country, using a special-event callsign, participating in a contest or operating under reciprocal arrangements. Listen carefully to the complete identification and check a reliable callsign database if you are unsure. Looking up a callsign Online callsign databases such as QRZ.com ↗ can provide information voluntarily published by operators. Regulatory databases may provide authoritative licensing information in some countries. A callsign lookup is useful, but never treat personal details from a database as an invitation to disclose them on air. Next step Once you can recognise and say callsigns confidently, see How to Make Your First Amateur Radio Contact for practical on-air examples. Written by Thomas Bernard — ZL3TOM Last updated: 5 September 2026 Accessibility and website feedback

content: ZL3TOM beginner guide Amateur Radio From Your Phone: Apps, EchoLink, AllStar, APRS and More Use a phone for amateur radio with EchoLink, QSO One, RepeaterPhone, Peanut, APRS, QRZ logging, Zello/network radios, remote stations and other useful tools. ← All guides Your phone can be a serious radio companion A phone can help you communicate through internet-linked amateur systems, find repeaters, track APRS, log contacts, look up callsigns, control remote equipment and monitor propagation. Some activities are radio support tools; others can carry your voice into an amateur-radio network. EchoLink EchoLink lets validated amateur operators connect to other users, repeaters and link nodes. Official mobile options are available, and your phone can be an EchoLink node in its own right. After validation, you can search for ZL3TOM-L , EchoLink node 304602 , as a practical node to try. My link is associated with my multimode system and may also be connected into ANZEL Radio ↗ . QSO One QSO One brings several linked voice systems into one interface and can be useful for operators who want access to systems such as EchoLink, AllStarLink, DMR, System Fusion and M17 from a supported device. Follow its current official platform and account requirements. RepeaterPhone on iPhone and iPad RepeaterPhone ↗ is designed for licensed amateur operators on Apple devices. It supports connections to EchoLink and AllStarLink nodes, directory searching, favourites, Bluetooth audio and Apple Watch PTT controls. You need the appropriate EchoLink or AllStarLink account. Peanut Peanut is a PTT client for licensed amateurs that connects to the Peanut server and rooms; some rooms are linked to D-STAR, Fusion and DMR reflectors. It requires a Peanut access code. See the dedicated Peanut guide on this site for setup and operating information. APRS APRS apps and web tools can show station positions, messages and other packet information. APRS.fi is useful for viewing stations, while platform-specific apps may provide transmit or messaging features. Think about privacy before beaconing a precise location. Logging and QRZ Your phone browser can access QRZ and many web logbooks, making it easy to look up callsigns and enter contacts while portable. Record UTC time, callsign, band and mode accurately. For offline or portable operation, choose a logger that can export standard ADIF files. Zello and network radio Zello and similar PTT services can turn a normal smartphone into a network-radio client. These internet conversations are different from direct RF amateur transmissions, although some communities operate authorised links into amateur systems. Remote stations Remote-control systems can let a licensed operator control a real amateur transceiver over the internet. Because the transmitter is real RF equipment, you must follow the licence rules applying to the station and transmitter location, as well as the remote service's rules. Other useful phone tools Consider repeater directories, propagation and solar-weather tools, satellite pass predictors, Maidenhead grid locators, antenna calculators, digital-mode references, band-plan references, Morse practice, SDR receivers and club/net calendars. content: ZL3TOM beginner guide Amateur Radio in New Zealand: Beginner Guide Get started with amateur radio in New Zealand: find a local club, explore Ham Cram training, and learn about the GAOC, callsigns and your first station. ← All guides 01 How amateur licensing works in New Zealand New Zealand amateur operators share a General User Radio Licence (GURL) . You do not apply for a separate station licence or pay an individual radio-licence fee, but you must hold a current General Amateur Operator's Certificate (GAOC) and callsign before transmitting. The GURL sets the legal conditions for ordinary amateur operation. It does not authorise every activity: beacons, repeaters and fixed links have separate licensing arrangements. 02 Get your certificate and callsign Start by contacting your local amateur radio club. Use the NZART branch and club directory ↗ to find a club near you. Ask about learning the theory, training options and arranging your examination and callsign. Contact your local club and ask which learning and examination options are available in your area. Study the radio theory, regulations and safe operating practices covered by the amateur examination. Check the NZART Ham Cram calendar ↗ for intensive training events, and contact the organising club about bookings, preparation, fees and examination arrangements. Ask your club to help you arrange an examination with an approved examiner. You can also check the Approved Radio Examiner information from RSM ↗ . Sit the examination and follow the examiner's current process for obtaining your certificate and callsign. Check that your certificate and callsign are recorded in the Register of Radio Frequencies before transmitting. Training, examination or callsign-processing fees may apply. Ask the club or examiner about costs before booking; the shared GURL itself has no individual licence fee. NZART study guides and practice exams → 03 Choose a sensible first station A VHF/UHF handheld is an accessible way to learn local simplex and repeater operation. Before buying, check which repeaters and activity are actually available around your QTH. An external antenna often improves a handheld more than extra transmitter power. HF opens longer-distance contacts but needs more space, antenna planning and attention to propagation. Start with equipment you can operate safely and learn well. 04 Know the difference between rules and band plans The RSM GURL provides the legal authority and conditions. The NZART band plan coordinates how amateurs use the available spectrum so different activities can coexist. Check both before transmitting. Always check the live documents: allocations, conditions and coordinated calling or repeater channels can change. A saved screenshot may be out of date. 05 Make your first call Program the correct frequency, mode, repeater offset and access tone where required. Listen long enough to be sure the channel is free. Give your callsign clearly and say that you are listening. Keep the first transmission short and leave a pause between overs. Write down the other station's callsign and contact details. SIMPLE FIRST CALL ZL3TOM listening. 06 Build good habits from day one Use the minimum power needed for a reliable contact. Identify with your callsign and keep transmissions courteous. Learn RF exposure, electrical and antenna safety before installing equipment. Join a local club or listen to experienced operators. Keep the current RSM licence conditions and NZART band plan bookmarked. title: What Does 73 Mean? Amateur Radio Slang Explained | ZL3TOM
description: What 73, 88, QTH, QSO, QSL, QRZ, QRM, QRN, RST, CQ and other ham radio terms mean, with simple examples for new amateur radio operators.
keywords: what does 73 mean amateur radio, ham radio slang, amateur radio terms, QTH meaning, QSO meaning, QSL meaning, QRZ meaning, QRM meaning, QRN meaning, RST report, CQ meaning
content: ZL3TOM amateur radio guide What Does 73 Mean? Amateur Radio Slang Explained What 73, 88, QTH, QSO, QSL, QRZ, QRM, QRN, RST, CQ and other ham radio terms mean, with simple examples for new amateur radio operators. ← All guides What does 73 mean in amateur radio? 73 means “best regards” and is one of the most common expressions in amateur radio. Operators often use it when finishing a contact, in messages and when signing an amateur-radio email. You normally say “seven three”, not “seventy-three”. EXAMPLE Thanks for the QSO. 73 from ZL3TOM. What does 88 mean? 88 traditionally means “love and kisses”. It is much less universal than 73, so use it only when it suits the relationship and context. Common Q codes and radio terms Term Plain-English meaning CQ A general call inviting any station to reply. QSO A radio contact or conversation between stations. QTH Your location or station location. QSL Confirmation that information or a contact has been received; also used for QSL cards and electronic confirmations. QRZ? “Who is calling me?” It is also the name of the well-known callsign database QRZ.com. QRM Interference from other stations or human-made radio signals. QRN Natural atmospheric/static noise affecting reception. QSY Change frequency. QRP Low-power operation. QRT Stop transmitting / close the station. RST signal reports RST stands for Readability, Strength and Tone. Voice contacts commonly use the first two values, such as “five nine”. CW contacts can use all three. A 59 report means readability 5 and signal strength 9; it should describe the signal you actually receive rather than being an automatic greeting. Other words beginners hear DX generally means long-distance radio communication. A net is an organised on-air gathering. An OM is an old traditional abbreviation for “old man” used between operators, while YL means “young lady”. Elmer is an informal term for an experienced amateur who mentors another operator. 73s is often heard conversationally, although the established radiotelegraph abbreviation is simply 73. Do you need to use radio slang? No. Clear everyday language is usually better than forcing Q codes into a voice conversation. Learn the common terms so you understand other operators, but do not worry about sounding like an expert on your first contact. Try the terms on air When you are ready, read my first amateur radio contact guide for examples of calling CQ, answering another station, exchanging signal reports and ending a QSO. content: ZL3TOM guide Antenna Basics Simple antenna fundamentals that help you get better results without overcomplicating your station. All guides 01 The antenna matters most A better antenna system usually improves results more than upgrading radios. Start simple, get on air, then improve one thing at a time. 02 Three basics that always help Height helps, especially for VHF and UHF. Clear space helps — stay away from metal roofs, gutters, and power lines. Good feedline helps, especially on VHF and above where coax loss can be high. 03 Coax and connectors Choose coax that suits the run length and band. Weatherproof every outdoor join. Use strain relief so connectors do not carry weight. 04 Understanding SWR Low SWR can protect your radio and keep power transfer efficient. Perfect SWR does not guarantee performance; pattern and height matter too. If SWR is high, stop and check connectors, coax, and antenna length. ON-AIR EXAMPLE Fix safety and reliability first, tune for SWR second, then chase performance. 05 Safety comes first Keep antennas well clear of power lines — always. Secure masts and guy lines for serious wind loads. Plan grounding and lightning protection for your situation. title: APRS for Beginners: Radio, Apps and APRS.fi | ZL3TOM
description: Learn what APRS does, how stations exchange position and status information, ways to receive or transmit, and how to use APRS.fi responsibly.
keywords: APRS for beginners, APRS.fi, APRSdroid, amateur packet radio, APRS beacon, APRS callsign SSID, ZL3TOM APRS
content: ZL3TOM beginner guide APRS for Beginners: Radio, Apps and APRS.fi Learn what APRS does, how stations exchange position and status information, ways to receive or transmit, and how to use APRS.fi responsibly. ← All guides 01 APRS is more than a moving map APRS—the Automatic Packet Reporting System—exchanges local, real-time amateur-radio information. Position reports are familiar, but the system also supports station status, short messages, objects, weather data and queries using standard packet formats. 02 Start by receiving Open APRS.fi ↗ and search for a callsign or your local area. Watching stations first helps you understand symbols, paths, comments and how often different station types beacon. A receive-capable radio and packet decoder can also show local RF activity without transmitting. 03 Ways to use APRS APRS-capable radio: combines a radio, GPS and packet modem in one unit. Radio plus TNC: a separate terminal node controller or sound-card modem encodes and decodes packets. Phone app: software such as APRSdroid can display or gate information using supported radio or internet connections. Web map: APRS.fi is useful for viewing data that has reached the APRS-IS internet system. 04 Configure a station carefully Enter your own licensed callsign and choose an appropriate SSID for the station type. Select the frequency and packet settings specified by the current local band plan. Choose a symbol and short comment that accurately describe the station. Use a conservative beacon rate and a path suited to the local network. Test locally and check whether your packets are being heard. Long or aggressive paths and rapid beacons can congest the shared channel. Follow local digipeater guidance. 05 Protect privacy and safety Remember: APRS position reports may become publicly visible and remain available through internet services. Do not beacon a private home location, vulnerable person, or sensitive journey without informed permission. Keep attention on driving, mount equipment safely and never operate a phone by hand while moving. 06 If your station does not appear Confirm your callsign, SSID, symbol and packet format. Check the local frequency, audio level and squelch. Listen for packet activity and confirm an iGate is within range. Reduce path complexity while testing. Remember that APRS.fi only shows packets that reach APRS-IS; absence from the map does not always mean no RF station heard you. Official sources Software and network details change. content: ZL3TOM guide Audio and Levels Quick, practical settings and habits for clean audio on SSB, FM, CW, and digital modes. All guides 01 The goal: sound clean On every mode, the easiest station to work is the station that sounds clean and steady. Loud does not equal good — clean equals good. 02 SSB mic gain and processing Set mic gain so your voice is strong but not distorted. Use compression or speech processing lightly. Keep a consistent mic distance and speak across the mic to reduce pops. ON-AIR EXAMPLE If people say you are splattering or your audio is crunchy, reduce gain or processing. 03 FM and handheld habits Use a normal voice and normal mic distance. Talking too close often causes muffled audio or clipping. On repeaters, key up, pause, then talk. 04 Digital drive level Start with low audio drive and increase slowly. Aim for minimal or no ALC movement on many radios. Turn off speech processing for sound-card digital modes. ON-AIR EXAMPLE Clean digital beats extra power, every time. 05 Quick checklist ON-AIR EXAMPLE SSB: no distortion, light processing FM: normal deviation, do not shout Digital: low drive, minimal ALC All: steady pace, clear callsign Written by Thomas Bernard — ZL3TOM Last updated: 3 September 2026 Accessibility and website feedback Good operating Listen first. title: Amateur Radio Hotspots Explained: Pi-Star, WPSD, DMR and Digital Voice | ZL3TOM
description: A beginner guide to amateur radio hotspots, Pi-Star, WPSD, DMR, D-STAR, YSF and M17, including how hotspots work and how they differ from repeaters.
keywords: amateur radio hotspot explained, DMR hotspot, Pi-Star hotspot, WPSD hotspot, digital voice hotspot, D-Star hotspot, YSF hotspot, M17 hotspot, ham radio hotspot beginner
content: ZL3TOM amateur radio guide Amateur Radio Hotspots Explained: Pi-Star, WPSD, DMR and Digital Voice A beginner guide to amateur radio hotspots, Pi-Star, WPSD, DMR, D-STAR, YSF and M17, including how hotspots work and how they differ from repeaters. ← All guides What is an amateur radio hotspot? A digital-voice hotspot is a small personal gateway between a compatible radio and an internet-connected digital voice network. Your handheld normally makes a short-range RF connection to the hotspot; the hotspot then carries the digital voice traffic over the internet to the selected network, reflector, room or talkgroup. What equipment is inside? Many hotspots combine a small computer, such as a Raspberry Pi or similar board, with an MMDVM-compatible radio modem. Some are complete commercial devices. The modem handles the local digital RF side while software manages networking, modes and configuration. Pi-Star and WPSD Pi-Star became a widely used hotspot and repeater software platform for digital voice. WPSD is another dashboard/software distribution used with compatible hotspots and digital voice systems. These are software platforms rather than radio networks themselves: the configured hotspot can connect onward to supported networks and protocols. DMR hotspots With DMR, a hotspot can connect your DMR handheld to services such as BrandMeister or other supported DMR networks. Configuration can involve your callsign, DMR ID, local hotspot frequency, colour code, timeslot/network settings and network credentials where required. Use a legal, appropriate frequency and the current instructions for your country and network. D-STAR, YSF and M17 Compatible hotspot hardware and software may support several modes, including D-STAR, Yaesu System Fusion/YSF and M17. Support depends on the modem, firmware, software and network. Cross-mode features may also exist, but they do not mean every network or mode is automatically interconnected. Hotspot versus repeater Personal hotspot Repeater Usually intended for short-range personal access. Usually designed to cover a wider local or regional area. Often owned and configured by one operator. Often operated for a club or wider amateur community. Commonly uses low RF power. Uses dedicated repeater equipment, antennas and coordinated operating arrangements where applicable. Internet connectivity is normally central to network access. May provide local RF communication and may also be internet-linked. Simple connection path TYPICAL HOTSPOT PATH Your digital handheld → RF → personal hotspot → Internet → digital voice network → other users/repeaters/hotspots Do I need a hotspot? A hotspot can be useful when you cannot reach a suitable digital repeater, want personal access to a digital network, or want to experiment with supported modes. If a good local repeater already provides the network access you need, a hotspot may not be necessary. Important setup tips Use your own valid callsign and required network ID. Choose an appropriate legal hotspot frequency for your location. Keep firmware and hotspot software maintained. Use strong unique passwords for dashboards and network services. Do not expose an administration dashboard directly to the public internet without appropriate protection. Check network rules before enabling bridges or cross-mode functions. What should I learn next? If DMR is your main interest, continue with the digital voice beginner guide and getting a DMR ID . For internet-linked voice options beyond a hotspot, see the internet-linked radio networks guide . title: Digital Voice for Beginners: DMR, D-STAR, C4FM and M17 | ZL3TOM
description: A plain-language beginner guide to amateur radio digital voice, comparing DMR, D-STAR, System Fusion C4FM and M17, plus talkgroups, reflectors and hotspots.
keywords: digital voice amateur radio beginners, DMR vs D-STAR vs C4FM, System Fusion, M17, talkgroups reflectors hotspots, ZL3TOM
content: ZL3TOM beginner guide Digital Voice for Beginners: DMR, D-STAR, C4FM and M17 A plain-language beginner guide to amateur radio digital voice, comparing DMR, D-STAR, System Fusion C4FM and M17, plus talkgroups, reflectors and hotspots. ← All guides 01 What digital voice means A digital voice radio converts microphone audio into data, sends that data by radio, and turns it back into speech at the receiver. The radio signal is still RF; internet links may then connect repeaters, hotspots and rooms around the world. Digital voice can sound clean when the signal is adequate, but near the coverage limit it may break up or disappear rather than gradually becoming noisy like analogue FM. 02 DMR Digital Mobile Radio is widely used by amateur operators. You will meet DMR IDs, talkgroups, time slots, colour codes and codeplugs. BrandMeister and TGIF are examples of networks; their accounts and talkgroup behaviour are separate. DMR can be powerful but has the most terminology at the start. Get your DMR ID before programming a network-connected setup. 03 D-STAR D-STAR means Digital Smart Technology for Amateur Radio. It is an open protocol created for amateur radio and supports callsign-based routing, repeaters and linked reflectors. Your callsign registration and routing fields need to be correct. Learn the local repeater's instructions before changing link commands. 04 System Fusion and C4FM System Fusion is Yaesu's digital system using C4FM modulation. Many compatible repeaters can automatically handle analogue FM and digital C4FM. WIRES-X links participating stations through rooms and nodes. A radio displaying C4FM does not automatically mean every internet network or room is available; the repeater or hotspot configuration also matters. 05 M17 M17 is an open digital radio protocol developed by the amateur radio community. It uses open technology for digital voice and data, with reflectors used for linking. Equipment and local coverage may be less common than DMR, D-STAR or System Fusion, so check what is active in your area. 06 Talkgroups, reflectors, rooms and hotspots Talkgroup A DMR conversation group selected by number. Reflector A shared connection point used by systems such as D-STAR and M17. Room A named WIRES-X destination used by System Fusion stations. Hotspot A small personal radio-and-internet gateway. Its RF frequency, mode, operator ID and network settings must be configured correctly. 07 Start without the confusion Find which mode has local repeaters, groups or friends you want to contact. Choose one mode first and learn its basic terms. Use a known-good codeplug or local club guidance as a reference, but verify every frequency and callsign field. Listen before transmitting and leave a pause between overs. Keep radio firmware, programming software and codeplug backups organised. Useful distinction: EchoLink and AllStar are linked voice systems, but they are not over-the-air digital modulation formats such as DMR, D-STAR, C4FM or M17. title: How to Install and Use EchoLink | ZL3TOM
description: A beginner-friendly EchoLink setup guide for Windows, Android, iPhone and the web, including callsign validation, audio checks and your first contact.
keywords: EchoLink setup, how to install EchoLink, EchoLink validation, EchoLink beginner guide, amateur radio apps, ZL3TOM
content: ZL3TOM beginner guide How to Install and Use EchoLink A beginner-friendly EchoLink setup guide for Windows, Android, iPhone and the web, including callsign validation, audio checks and your first contact. ← All guides 01 What EchoLink does EchoLink lets licensed amateur radio operators connect through internet-linked stations. You can use an app directly, or connect through a local repeater or link that is already on EchoLink. Callsigns ending in -L are link stations and -R identifies repeater stations. A plain callsign is normally an individual user. 02 Choose the official version EchoLink is available from the official site for Windows, Android and iOS, with EchoLink Web available in a browser. Download from the official source rather than an unofficial app store listing or download mirror. Start here: Official EchoLink downloads and web access ↗ 03 Register and validate your callsign Install and open EchoLink, then enter your amateur radio callsign. Choose a strong password that you do not reuse elsewhere. Complete the official validation process and provide the requested proof of licence. Wait until your callsign is approved before trying to connect. EchoLink access is for licensed amateur radio operators. Use your own callsign and keep your licence details current. 04 Set up clear audio Allow microphone access when your phone or computer asks. Select the correct microphone and speaker or headset. Keep the microphone level moderate; loud or distorted audio is harder to understand. Use headphones if speaker audio is feeding back into the microphone. Listen to a conversation before transmitting. On a linked network, leave a short pause after the other station unkeys so links can reset and another operator can join. 05 Make your first connection Search by callsign, location or node number. Select a station and connect. Listen first and check the channel is free. Press transmit, pause briefly, then give your callsign and say you are listening. Release transmit fully when you finish each over. Disconnect when your contact is complete. ON-AIR EXAMPLE ZL3TOM listening through EchoLink. 06 Common EchoLink problems Callsign not accepted Complete validation and make sure the callsign matches your licence. No audio Check microphone permission, input/output device selection and system volume. Cannot connect Try another station and the app's relay or proxy option. Some routers and networks restrict direct connections. Echo or feedback Use headphones and lower speaker or microphone volume. 07 Try ZL3TOM-L Once your EchoLink callsign is validated and your audio is working, you can search for ZL3TOM-L , node 304602 , in Christchurch, New Zealand. It is my EchoLink link and is part of my multimode setup. The link may also be connected into ANZEL Radio ↗ , so listen first before transmitting and leave a pause between overs. FIRST CALL EXAMPLE ZL3TOM, this is [your callsign], testing through EchoLink. Official sources Software and network details change. content: ZL3TOM guide Emergency Comms Basics Clear, calm habits for message passing, priority traffic, and directed nets. All guides 01 The goal: clear communication In emergency-style traffic, clarity and calm matter more than radio jargon. Keep messages short, accurate, and confirmed. 02 Directed nets The net control station manages the flow; wait to be called in. Use short transmissions, identify clearly, then stand by. If you double with someone, stop and try again when invited. ON-AIR EXAMPLE Net control, ZL3TOM, Christchurch, no traffic. 03 Message handling Record who it is to, who it is from, and the message content. Repeat names, addresses, phone numbers, and counts. Read back key parts and confirm what you copied. ON-AIR EXAMPLE To: [name or agency] From: [name or station] Message: [short, clear content] Time: [UTC] Date: [UTC] 04 Priority and emergency breaks Use priority or emergency breaks only when genuinely needed. Keep the wording short so net control can respond quickly. ON-AIR EXAMPLE Break, priority traffic Break, emergency traffic 05 Voice discipline Use phonetics for names and locations when copy is weak. Pause between overs, especially on linked systems. If you are relaying, clearly say so and identify who you are relaying for. Never guess callsigns, names, or numbers. title: How to Make Your First Amateur Radio Contact | ZL3TOM
description: Exactly what to say on your first amateur radio contact, including calling CQ, answering a CQ, callsigns, signal reports, repeaters, digital voice and ending a QSO.
content: ZL3TOM beginner guide How to Make Your First Amateur Radio Contact Exactly what to say on your first amateur radio contact, including calling CQ, answering a CQ, callsigns, signal reports, repeaters, digital voice and ending a QSO. ← All guides Before you transmit Check that you are authorised to transmit, choose a permitted frequency and mode, set sensible power, then listen before pressing PTT. On a repeater or linked system, listen long enough to understand whether a conversation or net is already in progress. Your callsign is your on-air identity Say your callsign clearly. Do not rush it. If the other operator misses part of it, use the international phonetic alphabet. For example: Zulu Lima Three Tango Oscar Mike . Calling CQ on HF EXAMPLE CQ CQ CQ, this is ZL3TOM, Zulu Lima Three Tango Oscar Mike, calling CQ and listening. Pause and listen. If nobody answers, call again. Avoid endlessly repeating CQ without giving listeners time to reply. Answering a CQ EXAMPLE [Their callsign], this is ZL3TOM, Zulu Lima Three Tango Oscar Mike. Once acknowledged, exchange names, locations and a signal report. Keep your first contact simple; you do not need to know every piece of radio jargon. Signal reports For voice contacts, R-S reports describe readability and signal strength. A report such as 5 by 9 means perfectly readable with a very strong signal. Give the report you actually observe rather than automatically saying 59. Repeaters and FM You normally do not call CQ repeatedly on a local repeater. Listen first, then identify and say you are listening. REPEATER EXAMPLE ZL3TOM listening. If joining an existing conversation, wait for the pause between stations and identify. Leave a short gap between overs so another station can break in. Digital voice and linked systems On DMR, EchoLink, AllStar, System Fusion, M17 and other linked systems, key up and pause briefly before speaking so the network has time to establish the audio path. Large talkgroups may reach many repeaters and users, so keep test transmissions short. DMR EXAMPLE ZL3TOM listening on Talkgroup 91. What to talk about A first QSO can be as simple as callsign, name, location, signal report and the equipment you are using. Ask the other operator about their station or local conditions. Normal friendly conversation is fine. Ending the QSO EXAMPLE Thanks for the contact. 73 from ZL3TOM. Clear and listening. On HF you can simply thank the station, exchange 73 and identify. On a linked node, disconnect only if you made the connection and local practice requires it. Afterwards Write down the other callsign, UTC date and time, band, mode and any useful notes. You can then enter the contact into your preferred logbook and, where appropriate, request or confirm a QSL. Keep learning Operating basics Build confident operating habits. content: ZL3TOM beginner guide How to Get a DMR ID for Amateur Radio Learn what a DMR ID is, how licensed amateur radio operators register through RadioID, and where to enter the ID in a radio, hotspot and BrandMeister account. ← All guides 01 What a DMR ID is A DMR ID is a numeric identity associated with a licensed amateur radio operator. Digital Mobile Radio networks use it to identify your transmissions and display your callsign information. Your callsign remains your legal on-air identification. The number does not replace good operating practice or the requirements of your local licence. 02 Register through RadioID Go to the official RadioID website ↗ . Create an account using your real details and licensed callsign. Follow the current application process and upload the licence evidence requested for your country. Check every entry before submitting; your callsign and identity need to match the evidence. Wait for approval, then record your assigned ID somewhere safe. The website and verification steps can change. Follow the instructions shown by RadioID rather than an old screenshot or unofficial video. 03 Put the ID in the right places DMR radio: enter the ID in your radio's codeplug or programming software. Hotspot: set the same operator ID in the hotspot dashboard. Do not copy another operator's number. Network account: if you use BrandMeister, create or update your self-care profile with the same callsign and ID. Software app: enter your ID only where the official app documentation requests it. Back up your codeplug before editing it, and confirm the radio shows your own ID before transmitting. 04 DMR terms you will meet Talkgroup A numbered conversation group, such as worldwide BrandMeister talkgroup 91. Time slot On many DMR repeaters, two independent voice paths share one radio channel. Use the slot specified by the repeater or talkgroup plan. Colour code A DMR access setting, similar in purpose to a repeater access tone. It must match the repeater. Codeplug The saved radio configuration containing channels, contacts, zones and your DMR ID. 05 Protect your accounts Use a unique password for RadioID and each network account. Never publish hotspot security passwords or IAX credentials. Use the official password-reset process if access is lost. Update your record if your callsign changes. 06 Your first DMR contact Load a known local repeater or hotspot channel, select the correct talkgroup, and listen before transmitting. Key up, pause briefly, give your callsign, and say you are listening. Leave extra space between overs because linked networks need time to switch. ON-AIR EXAMPLE ZL3TOM listening on talkgroup 91. content: ZL3TOM beginner guide HF CQ and Contacts Practical tips for HF calling, answering, handling busy conditions, and finishing a QSO cleanly. ← All guides 01 1. Find a clear frequency Listen for at least 10 to 20 seconds — longer if conditions are busy or weak. Check whether the frequency is used for a net, DX activity, or a common calling spot. If you are unsure, ask once, then listen again. ON-AIR EXAMPLE Is this frequency in use, is this frequency in use, ZL3TOM. 02 Watch: How I Call CQ Jim - W6LG demonstrates how he calls CQ in this Ham Radio Basics video. Video credit: Jim - W6LG on YouTube ↗ 03 Watch: What is SSB and How to Tune in SSB Jim - W6LG explains what single sideband (SSB) is and demonstrates how to tune an SSB signal so speech sounds natural. Video credit: Jim - W6LG on YouTube ↗ 04 2. Calling CQ on SSB Short beats fancy. Repeat your callsign clearly, then listen rather than calling constantly. ON-AIR EXAMPLE CQ CQ CQ, this is ZL3TOM, ZL3TOM calling CQ and standing by. 05 3. Answering a CQ Say their callsign once, then your callsign once. Slow is smooth; smooth is fast. ON-AIR EXAMPLE ZL3ABC, this is ZL3TOM. 06 4. Your first over Make the contact easy to log: confirm callsigns, then give a report, your name, and your location. ON-AIR EXAMPLE ZL3ABC, thanks for the call. You are 5 and 9 in Christchurch. Name Thomas, over. 07 5. Signal reports Give a report that feels fair. For a weak signal, explain kindly: ‘You are 4 and 7, readable with a bit of noise.’ Ask for repeats when needed — never guess a callsign. 08 6. Handling pileups Take one station at a time and confirm the callsign before logging. Keep overs short so the frequency keeps flowing. If you cannot copy, ask for the callsign again. ON-AIR EXAMPLE Only the station ending in ABC, again please. 09 7. End cleanly Thank the operator, confirm final callsigns, and say whether you are staying on frequency. ON-AIR EXAMPLE Thanks for the contact, 73. This is ZL3TOM clear and listening. Official sources Software and network details change. description: A practical guide to the International Radio Network, ANZEL multimode network, ZMR Radio, Network Radios and Zello, including how the systems connect and where to get current access information.
keywords: International Radio Network, IRN radio, ANZEL network, ANZEL Radio, ZMR Radio, Network Radios, Zello radio, VoIP amateur radio, RoIP amateur radio, ZL3TOM
content: ZL3TOM linked radio guide Internet-linked radio networks: IRN, ANZEL, ZMR and Network Radios How Zello, network radios and multimode VoIP/RoIP systems fit together, plus the official places to find current connection and registration details. ← All guides 01 What internet-linked radio networks are Internet-linked radio networks carry voice between operators, apps, radio-style devices, repeaters, gateways and other linked systems. Depending on the network, you may use a phone app such as Zello, a dedicated network radio, a DMR talkgroup, an EchoLink or AllStar connection, or another supported gateway. These systems are useful for keeping radio communities connected across long distances, but each network has its own rules, registration process and connection methods. Always use the current information from the network itself. 02 International Radio Network (IRN) The International Radio Network (IRN) ↗ says its mission is to promote the amateur radio hobby and welcomes both licensed and non-licensed people who are interested in radio communications. Its website provides an FAQ, connection information, net schedules, registration and a live dashboard. Getting connected: use the official IRN website ↗ and follow its current registration and Connections information. Requirements can change, so do not rely on old connection details copied from another website. 03 ZMR Radio ZMR Radio ↗ describes itself as a partner of the International Radio Network and as a service that complements rather than replaces amateur radio. Its current site says it provides a welcoming radio environment using Zello and DMR talkgroups on the TGIF network, with channels for licensed amateurs as well as hobby radio enthusiasts. For current channel names, talkgroups and joining instructions, use ZMR's own website. That avoids stale channel information and makes sure you see its latest rules and access requirements. 04 Network Radios and Zello The Network Radios Channel Suite ↗ is built on the Zello push-to-talk platform. Network radios are usually internet-connected Android-style devices designed to feel more like a handheld or mobile radio, often with a physical PTT button, while Zello can also run directly on phones and other supported devices. The Network Radios website publishes its channel information, Zello hints and tips, hardware information and accessibility guidance. Start there when setting up a device or looking for the current channel suite. 05 ANZEL Radio Multimode Network The ANZEL Multimode VoIP / RoIP Network ↗ connects multiple radio-over-IP and digital systems. Its current website lists connections that include EchoLink conferences, AllStar nodes, IRLP, D-Star, DMR, YSF, M17 and other linked systems. ZL3TOM activity: my nodes are generally connected to this network for almost 24/7 activity. If you are looking for me, this is one of the best linked-network places to listen and call. Because a multimode network can change links and gateways over time, use the ANZEL website for its live network map, current connection numbers, net calendar and operating information. 06 How the connections fit together You do not necessarily need the same app or radio as another operator. A network may bridge several technologies so that audio entering through one supported system can be heard on another. For example, one person may arrive through Zello or a network-radio channel while another uses an amateur-radio gateway supported by that particular network. Bridging is controlled by the network administrators. Never assume that every channel, talkgroup or reflector is permanently linked. Check the network's dashboard, connection page or map before troubleshooting your own equipment. 07 Good operating on linked networks Listen before transmitting and make sure a conversation is not already in progress. Leave a short pause between overs so linked gateways have time to switch and another operator can join. Use your callsign where amateur-radio rules require it and follow the rules of the network you are using. Do not share private node, IAX, administrator or account credentials. Remember that some networks also include non-licensed users, so the operating environment may differ from an amateur-only repeater. Use the official network website for current access details rather than copying passwords, codes or channel information from unofficial posts. 08 Where to start Network Best starting point International Radio Network irn.radio ↗ ZMR Radio ZMR website ↗ Network Radios Network Radios Channel Suite ↗ ANZEL Radio anzel.radio ↗ Read the current registration, connections and conduct information on each site before transmitting or linking a node. content: ZL3TOM beginner guide How to Log Amateur Radio Contacts on QRZ A step-by-step QRZ Logbook guide covering contact details, confirmation matching, UTC time, editing, ADIF imports and linked-network notes. ← All guides 01 Write down the contact first Record the other station's callsign, UTC date and time, band, mode, signal report and any useful notes. UTC avoids confusion between time zones and date changes. Check the callsign while the contact is still fresh. 02 Add a QSO in QRZ Logbook Sign in to QRZ and open your logbook. Select Enter Call or use the Add QSO option from a callsign page. Enter the contacted callsign. Complete the sender, receiver and QSL information requested. Check the UTC date, time, band and mode carefully. Save the record. QRZ's screens can change, so use its current help pages if a button has moved. 03 How QRZ confirmation matching works Each operator logs the QSO independently. QRZ matches key information including both callsigns, the UTC date and time, band and mode. Its current guide allows a time difference of up to 30 minutes, but entering the most accurate time gives the best chance of a clean match. 04 EchoLink, DMR, QSO One and linked contacts Log the actual contact details consistently and use the comments or notes field to record the network, talkgroup, room or node—for example EchoLink 304602, DMR TG 91, AllStar 40452 or QSO One. Agree on the details: QRZ confirmation depends on matching band and mode. For an internet-only contact without a normal RF band, check QRZ's current accepted fields and agree with the other operator on what both of you will record. 05 Correct mistakes carefully QRZ says a logged callsign cannot be edited; if it is wrong, delete the record and enter it again. Fields used by an already confirmed match can also be restricted. Review the official FAQ before changing a confirmed QSO. 06 Import with ADIF and keep a backup If another logger exports ADIF, use QRZ Logbook's Settings and Import function. Check your callsign, date range and time handling before importing a large file. Keep the original ADIF as a backup and inspect the import report for duplicates or rejected records. title: Network Radios Explained: Are They Amateur Radio? | ZL3TOM
description: Understand network radios, Zello push-to-talk, Wi-Fi and mobile-data radios, how they differ from RF amateur transceivers, and how communities such as IRN and ZMR use them.
content: ZL3TOM beginner guide Network Radios Explained: Are They Amateur Radio? Understand network radios, Zello push-to-talk, Wi-Fi and mobile-data radios, how they differ from RF amateur transceivers, and how communities such as IRN and ZMR use them. ← All guides What is a network radio? A network radio is usually a phone-like or dedicated push-to-talk device that sends voice over the internet rather than directly over an amateur RF frequency. Devices can use Wi-Fi or cellular data such as 4G and 5G. Many resemble handheld radios and have a physical PTT button. Is a network radio amateur radio? The device itself is not necessarily transmitting on an amateur RF band. A Zello-to-Zello conversation is internet voice/PTT. However, internet systems can be connected to amateur-radio gateways, repeaters, reflectors or nodes. Once a path crosses onto amateur RF, amateur-radio licensing and operating requirements apply to that RF side and network rules may also restrict access to licensed operators. Zello and push-to-talk Zello turns compatible phones and network-radio devices into internet PTT clients. Communities can organise channels for conversation and, where authorised, gateways can link services together. Dedicated network-radio handsets Some Android-based handsets look like traditional portable radios but contain cellular/Wi-Fi hardware rather than an amateur VHF/UHF transmitter. A hardware PTT key, loud speaker and rugged body can make them feel more radio-like than a normal phone. IRN, ZMR and other communities The International Radio Network (IRN) provides an internet-linked radio community with several connection methods. ZMR — Zello Mode Radio — uses Zello and also has links into digital-radio systems. The Original Network Radios Channel Suite is another Zello-based network-radio community. Availability, rooms, gateways and access requirements change, so always use each network's current website. Current network information: IRN ↗ · ZMR ↗ · Network Radios ↗ · ANZEL Radio ↗ Network radio versus an RF handheld An RF handheld can communicate directly over radio spectrum and may work locally without the public internet. A network radio normally needs an IP connection and server/service infrastructure. The two worlds can meet through gateways, which is why it is important to know where your audio is being routed. Using QSO One with internet-linked radio If you want to explore amateur-radio systems from a phone or other supported device, also see my QSO One Guide . It explains how to get started with QSO One and use its supported linked-radio features. Good operating Read the channel rules, identify appropriately, listen before transmitting, avoid long tests on busy channels, leave gaps between overs and remember that a linked channel may have listeners on several different systems. content: ZL3TOM beginner guide New Zealand Amateur Radio Band Plans: Beginner Guide A beginner guide to New Zealand amateur radio band plans, legal licence conditions, common HF and VHF/UHF bands, modes and checks before transmitting. ← All guides 01 Licence conditions and band plans are different The RSM Amateur Radio Operators GURL is the legal authority for eligible New Zealand amateurs to transmit. The NZART band plan is the operating coordination guide used to reduce interference between modes and activities. A band-plan segment is not permission by itself. Your certificate, the current GURL, equipment and any location-specific restriction still control what you may legally do. 02 A quick orientation to common bands Band Common beginner uses 80 m and 40 m Regional and longer-range HF voice, CW and digital contacts. 30 m, 20 m and 17 m HF CW, data and international contacts; mode permissions differ by band. 15 m, 12 m and 10 m Long-distance contacts when propagation supports them. 6 m VHF weak-signal, local and occasional long-distance activity. 2 m and 70 cm Local simplex, repeaters, satellites and digital voice. 23 cm and above Repeaters, data, satellites and microwave experimentation. This table is only an orientation. Use the current NZART plan for actual frequencies, bandwidths, calling channels and repeater allocations. 03 Read the plan before choosing a frequency Find the correct band and mode section. Check the authorised frequency range in the current GURL. Check the NZART plan for calling frequencies and coordinated mode segments. Allow for the full occupied bandwidth of your signal, especially near a band edge. Listen for existing activity and identify any local repeater input or output. 04 HF, VHF and UHF need different habits On HF, propagation, signal bandwidth and international band planning matter. On VHF/UHF, correct repeater offsets, access tones, simplex channels and local coordination are common concerns. Satellite operation needs Doppler adjustment and careful power use. The NZART band-usage guide complements the printable plan and explains recommended operating practices for New Zealand. 05 Be especially careful with special allocations Do not assume that a band available in another country has identical New Zealand conditions. Some allocations can have special power, mode, location or interference-protection requirements. The 60-metre area is one example where you should read the current GURL and NZART guidance before transmitting. 06 Five checks before you press PTT Am I authorised for this frequency and operation? Is my whole signal inside the permitted band? Am I following the current coordinated band plan? Is the frequency already in use? Are my power, antenna and station settings safe and appropriate? content: ZL3TOM beginner guide Peanut Amateur Radio App: Beginner Setup and Operating Guide A beginner guide to the Peanut amateur radio PTT app, including access codes, rooms, D-STAR/Fusion/DMR links, audio setup, first contacts and safe operating. ← All guides What Peanut is Peanut is an internet PTT application for amateur radio operators. The client connects to the Peanut server, which acts as a reflector where operators can meet. Some Peanut rooms are connected to D-STAR, System Fusion and DMR reflectors. What you need You need a valid amateur-radio callsign and a Peanut access code. Use the developer's current instructions because registration and room availability can change. Official information: PA7LIM Peanut information ↗ Install and prepare Use the official Peanut information page to find the current supported downloads. Install the app from the recommended source. Follow the developer's process to obtain the required code. Enter your own callsign and code. Allow microphone access and select suitable audio. Rooms and linked systems Choose a room and listen before transmitting. A room may be internet-only or may connect onward to an amateur digital reflector. Do not assume every room reaches RF. Check the current room list and information from the operator. Making a first call Listen first, press PTT, pause briefly, then identify with your callsign and say you are listening. Keep the first transmission short while you confirm audio and routing. EXAMPLE ZL3TOM listening through Peanut. Audio tips A headset can reduce feedback. Keep microphone gain moderate, avoid holding the phone too close to your mouth, and test on an appropriate room rather than repeatedly keying a busy linked reflector. Peanut versus EchoLink and AllStar They are separate systems. EchoLink has its own validated directory and RF link/repeater nodes; AllStarLink is based around linked Asterisk nodes; Peanut uses its own server and rooms, with some rooms bridged to digital reflectors. Your credentials for one system do not automatically grant access to another. Operating etiquette Use your callsign, leave gaps between overs, avoid monopolising linked rooms, respect room rules and remember that your audio may be heard on systems beyond the app itself. content: ZL3TOM beginner guide QSO One Setup Guide: DMR, EchoLink and AllStar A step-by-step QSO One guide for licensed amateur radio operators using EchoLink, AllStarLink, IAX Direct, DMR, System Fusion and M17 on Windows or Android. ← All guides 01 What QSO One is QSO One, developed by Frank KD8JKK, is a free internet voice client for licensed amateur radio operators. One app connects to AllStarLink, EchoLink, IAX Direct, DMR, System Fusion (YSF) and M17 on Windows or Android. It uses your device’s microphone, speaker and internet connection to receive and transmit through these networks without a separate radio, hotspot or Raspberry Pi. Depending on the destination, your voice may reach other app users, linked nodes or RF repeaters. It is useful at home, when travelling, or when a traditional radio setup is difficult to access. QSO One also provides directories, favourites, callsign lookup, contact logging and Net Finder. Access is free, with optional contributions to support development. You still need your amateur radio licence and any accounts required by your chosen network. 02 Download QSO One — now on Google Play New for Android: QSO One is now available from Google Play, making installation and updates much easier on Android devices. Start at the official QSO One website ↗ . Android: install QSO One from Google Play ↗ . Android 8.0 or later is supported. Windows: get QSO One from the Microsoft Store ↗ , or use the direct installer offered by QSO One. Install updates only from the official site, official app store or app updater. QSO One is currently available for Windows and Android. The official site lists iOS, macOS and Linux as coming soon. 03 QSO One video Watch this archived QSO One video for a visual introduction to the app and its amateur-radio network features. Watch QSO One on Internet Archive ↗ 04 How to use QSO One Once QSO One is installed, start with one network and learn the basic receive, connect and PTT controls before adding more. Create or sign in to QSO One using your amateur radio callsign. Choose a network such as AllStarLink, EchoLink, IAX Direct, DMR, System Fusion (YSF) or M17. Add the details that network requires. EchoLink requires a validated EchoLink account. DMR requires your own DMR ID and the credentials requested by your chosen network’s login card; see section 9 for the supported networks. IAX Direct requires credentials supplied by the node operator. Select your destination. Search for an AllStar node or EchoLink station, select a DMR talkgroup, or choose a YSF/M17 reflector. Listen first and make sure the destination is not already in use. Press and hold PTT to transmit. Pause briefly before speaking, identify with your callsign, and release PTT when finished. Disconnect when finished and log the QSO if you want to keep a record. SIMPLE FIRST CALL ZL3TOM listening through QSO One. On Android, QSO One can keep a session active in the background. Bluetooth, BLE and PoC hardware PTT devices are also supported. 05 Prepare your accounts QSO One: create or sign in with your licensed callsign as directed by the app. EchoLink: complete callsign validation first. DMR: obtain your own DMR ID from RadioID and configure the network account you intend to use. AllStarLink: use your authorised node details. IAX Direct credentials must come from the node owner. Keep secrets private: never publish an IAX password, hotspot security password or network account password. 06 First-run audio setup Allow microphone permission. Select the correct microphone and speaker or headset. Lower the microphone level if reports say your audio is distorted. Receive and listen before transmitting. Use headphones if you hear echo or feedback. Only one application should control the microphone at a time. 07 Connect with EchoLink Use your validated EchoLink callsign and EchoLink password, then search the directory for a station, link, repeater or conference. Save regular destinations as favourites, connect and listen before transmitting. QSO One supports direct UDP connections and automatic proxy fallback. A proxy can help on mobile data or connections where direct UDP is blocked. If a connection appears successful but carries no audio, try another proxy using the app’s controls. ZL3TOM EXAMPLE EchoLink node 304602 — ZL3TOM-L 08 Connect with AllStar or IAX Direct AllStarLink offers two connection methods: Node Mode: use your registered AllStarLink node number and credentials for a node connection. WT Mode (Web Transceiver): use your AllStarLink portal account without needing your own registered node. The destination must accept this connection method. Search the node directory, save favourites and connect to the destination. DTMF controls can operate supported node functions; follow the node operator’s instructions. IAX Direct connects to a particular server using the host, port, username and secret supplied by its operator. It supports stock ASL3, HamVOIP and legacy ASL2. These credentials are separate from your QSO One account. ZL3TOM EXAMPLE AllStar node 40452 09 Connect with DMR, System Fusion or M17 DMR: choose the network as well as the talkgroup QSO One supports more than BrandMeister and TGIF. The developer’s release notes confirm the following DMR network choices as checked on 6 October 2026: BrandMeister TGIF FreeDMR — introduced as experimental support. System X (FreeSTAR) — introduced as experimental support in version 4.0.4. AmComm — introduced as experimental support in version 4.0.4. VKDMR (Australia) — introduced as experimental support in version 4.0.4. DMR+ — introduced as experimental support in version 4.1.1. ADN Systems — introduced as experimental support in version 4.1.1, including live Last Heard. Keep the app current: experimental networks may have limitations. Check the current network picker and What’s new in your installed version. The official website’s older two-network description does not include all of these release additions. Obtain your own approved DMR ID from RadioID. Open DMR and select the network you want to use. Complete that network’s login card with your DMR ID and the credentials it requests. Password requirements differ between networks; your QSO One password is not automatically the network password. Choose an available server and the intended talkgroup. Check that network’s talkgroup directory rather than assuming a number has the same meaning on every network. Connect, confirm the destination and listen. Use Last Heard or Active Now where the selected network provides them; a live feed is not available on every network. Make a short identified transmission when clear, then release PTT and listen for a reply. A matching talkgroup number on two networks does not automatically join the same conversation. Any bridge between them depends on the network operators. System Fusion (YSF) Select System Fusion, use your licensed callsign and choose a YSF reflector from the directory. Save favourites and connect before using PTT. Where the reflector uses DG-ID groups, check your transmit and receive DG-ID settings so you send to and hear the intended group. YSF reflector access does not mean every WIRES-X room is directly available. M17 Select M17, choose a reflector and module, then connect and listen before transmitting. Your callsign identifies you; QSO One’s M17 connection does not require a separate network registration. M17 uses the open Codec 2 voice codec. Check the module because different modules may carry different conversations. 10 Useful current features Beyond making a connection, QSO One includes tools to help you find activity and keep track of contacts: Directories and favourites: search destinations and save the ones you use regularly. DMR activity: browse talkgroups and view supported live activity feeds. On networks with a live feed, tapping a Last Heard station can take you to its talkgroup. Scanning is network-dependent; check the controls available for your selected network. Net Finder: browse nets and connect to supported destinations. Version 4.1.1 added DMR+ and System X net entries. QSO logging: keep contact records and export ADIF for another logbook. Review imported contacts and record the actual internet/network path accurately. Callsign lookup: view available operator details from a callsign; the information depends on the underlying database. Received-audio recording: save received audio when enabled, with retention settings and starred recordings. PTT and audio: use the on-screen button, Windows spacebar, or compatible Bluetooth, BLE and PoC PTT hardware. Adjust your microphone and receive levels; automatic receive levelling helps with varying audio levels. Android background sessions: a foreground service keeps a connection running while switching apps or locking the screen. Reconnection logic helps when the network changes; check battery settings if your device stops the app. Features and hardware behaviour can vary with the app version, device and network. Start with the on-screen PTT button before configuring an external microphone or button. 11 Troubleshooting checklist Confirm your callsign validation or DMR ID approval is complete. Check microphone permission and selected audio devices. Verify the node number, talkgroup or destination. Re-enter private credentials carefully without sharing them. Try receive-only first and then one short transmission. Check the official QSO One site for current instructions and support. 12 Good linked-network operating Pause after keying, keep early transmissions short, and leave a gap between overs. Large talkgroups and linked nodes can cover many repeaters or users, so listen carefully and avoid long tests on busy destinations. FIRST CALL ZL3TOM listening through QSO One. content: ZL3TOM guide Repeaters and Nets Use amateur radio repeaters and participate in nets confidently, including AllStar and EchoLink linked systems. All guides 01 Repeater basics Listen first to make sure the repeater is clear. Key the microphone, pause for a second, then speak. Identify clearly and leave pauses between overs. Keep transmissions within the repeater timeout. 02 Monitoring and calling If nobody replies, wait and try once more. If the repeater is busy, keep transmissions short. ON-AIR EXAMPLE ZL3ABC, ZL3ABC, this is ZL3TOM. 03 Joining a conversation Wait for a clear gap, then say your callsign once. If invited in, keep your first over short. If it is a directed net or important traffic, stand by. 04 Linked systems Allow extra pauses for network delay. Keep topics appropriate for a wide audience. Avoid kerchunking; identify briefly if you key accidentally. Remember that many operators share the link. 05 Checking into a net Wait for net control to request check-ins. Give your callsign, location, and whether you have traffic. ON-AIR EXAMPLE Net control, ZL3TOM, Christchurch, no traffic. 06 Passing messages Write everything down before transmitting. Read back important details to confirm accuracy. Use phonetics for names, places, and numbers if copy is weak. content: ZL3TOM beginner guide USA Amateur Radio Band Plans: Beginner Guide A worldwide beginner guide to USA amateur radio bands, FCC licence classes, ARRL band plans, visiting privileges and working US stations from any country. ← All guides 01 Who this USA band-plan guide is for This guide is for anyone learning the United States amateur allocations: new US licensees, international operators working American stations, visitors planning to operate in the USA, and listeners following US-based nets or events. US privileges can differ from those in your own country. A US operator must stay within the frequencies, modes and power limits allowed by FCC rules and their licence class. 02 The three US licence classes Technician Entry-level privileges with broad VHF/UHF access and limited privileges on some HF bands. General Much wider HF privileges as well as VHF/UHF access. Amateur Extra The widest amateur privileges, including additional HF sub-band access. Always use the current FCC and ARRL information because exact frequency and mode privileges matter. 03 Common US amateur bands at a glance Range group Common bands Typical activity HF 160, 80, 40, 30, 20, 17, 15, 12 and 10 m Voice, CW, data and long-distance contacts, subject to class and mode limits. Low VHF 6 m Local, weak-signal and propagation openings. VHF 2 m and 1.25 m Simplex, repeaters, satellites and weak-signal work. UHF 70 cm and higher Repeaters, satellites, data, digital voice and experimentation. This is not a frequency-authorisation table. Consult the current ARRL chart and FCC Part 97 for the precise limits that apply. 04 Allocations and voluntary band plans FCC Part 97 contains the binding rules. ARRL band plans are voluntary operating arrangements that divide bands into commonly used mode and activity segments. Following them reduces avoidable interference, but they do not expand your legal privileges. 05 Avoid band-edge mistakes Check the operator's licence class and the exact authorised sub-band. Allow for the entire occupied signal, not just the displayed dial frequency. Check mode and emission restrictions. Use no more transmitter power than needed for reliable communication. Listen before calling and respect established activity. 06 Working US stations from another country You normally operate under the rules that apply at your transmitter, while the US station operates under FCC rules at theirs. Choose a frequency, mode and power level that both stations may legally use, use UTC when arranging or logging the QSO, and leave safe room for the full signal near band edges. If you plan to transmit while physically in the United States, check the current FCC rules and any reciprocal operating arrangements before you travel. Your home-country licence does not automatically grant every US privilege. Official sources Software and network details change. content: ZL3TOM beginner guide What Is Amateur Radio? A Beginner's Guide to Ham Radio A worldwide beginner introduction to amateur radio: what it is, licensing, callsigns, bands, repeaters, antennas and making a first contact. ← All guides 01 What amateur radio is Amateur radio , often called ham radio , is a technical and communications hobby where licensed operators communicate by radio, experiment with equipment and antennas, use analogue and digital modes, join nets and make contacts locally or around the world. 02 How this differs from the New Zealand guide This page is the general worldwide introduction. If you are in New Zealand and want country-specific information about the licence framework, callsigns and getting started locally, use Amateur Radio in New Zealand . 03 Do you need a licence? Transmitting on amateur-radio frequencies normally requires the appropriate licence or authorisation for your country. Rules and permitted frequencies vary internationally, so check your national regulator or recognised amateur-radio organisation. 04 What can you do? Amateur radio includes local VHF/UHF contacts, repeaters, HF long-distance communication, Morse code, digital data, digital voice, APRS, satellites, portable operation and internet-linked radio systems. 05 What is a callsign? A callsign identifies an amateur station or operator. Learn more in Amateur Radio Callsigns Explained . 06 Your first contact Listen first, learn basic operating etiquette and keep the first conversation simple. The dedicated first amateur radio contact guide gives practical examples of what to say. Keep learning All amateur radio guides Browse the complete ZL3TOM guide library. Always follow the regulations, equipment limits and operating practices that apply where you are located. What is a Maidenhead locator?
